analysis.one_liner: Guarantees public employees nationwide the right to unionize and bargain collectively with their state and local governments.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee on May 16, 2024 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create, for the first time, a nationwide floor of collective bargaining rights for state and local government workers. A federal agency would judge whether each state's laws protect the right to organize, elect a union, bargain over pay and working conditions, and resolve deadlocks through binding procedures like arbitration. States that fall short would have those rights enforced for their public employees by the Federal Labor Relations Authority, with court enforcement available. States that already protect these rights would keep their own systems. The bill never got a hearing or vote in the Senate committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Public employees — teachers, firefighters, police, sanitation workers, nurses, and other state and local government workers — in states that currently deny or limit union bargaining rights. They would gain a federally guaranteed right to organize, elect union representation, and bargain a written contract over pay, hours, and working conditions, enforceable in court with attorneys' fees available. Unions also gain members and dues as workers in those states gain access to representation.

how_it_helps.text: It creates a federal right for public employees and their supervisors to form, join, or assist a union and to bargain collectively over wages, hours, and working conditions through representatives of their own choosing.

States that already protect these rights are left alone; states that do not would have the Federal Labor Relations Authority run elections, set bargaining units, resolve complaints, and enforce the federal floor.

It requires binding resolution of bargaining deadlocks (such as arbitration), permits payroll deduction of union dues, bans employer interference with organizing, and gives workers a private right of action in federal court with possible attorneys' fees.
It balances the new rights with limits: strikes and lockouts that would disrupt emergency or public safety services are prohibited.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, which would lose unilateral control over wages and working conditions for public employees and would bear the cost of bargaining, arbitration, and potentially higher compensation. In states without strong labor laws, the federal government and taxpayers would fund the new enforcement machinery.

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state choices: states whose laws fall short would have the Federal Labor Relations Authority, not their own government, write and enforce union bargaining rules for their employees, which state officials argued is federal interference in state personnel decisions.

Stronger union bargaining over wages and staffing can raise costs for state and local governments, which ultimately are paid by taxpayers, and binding arbitration could take final decisions out of elected officials' hands.

The Federal Labor Relations Authority would need to judge every state's laws against a new federal standard, inviting years of litigation over whether each state 'substantially provides' the required rights.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—collective bargaining rights for the roughly half of public employees who currently lack them—would be substantial, and the bill tries to soften the cost to states by letting them keep their own systems if those meet the federal floor and by exempting small towns. The drawbacks are real: it shifts power over state labor law to a federal agency and courts, states lose flexibility over their own workforces, and taxpayers could face higher labor costs. But the bill never got a committee vote, so none of these tradeoffs were tested in debate; the outcome is simply that the status quo—no federal bargaining rights for most state and local workers—continues.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Mazie Hirono introduced the bill on May 16, 2024, with 36 total cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments in states without strong union laws keep the power to set pay and working conditions unilaterally; opponents of expanding public-sector unionism gained by doing nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State governments; opponents of public-sector unions

for.name: 36 Senate cosponsors (35 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.role: Cosponsors including Sen. Chuck Schumer (Majority Leader), Sen. Bernie Sanders, and Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred on May 16, 2024.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 supporters were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled agenda never advanced it.

industries.note: The bill would give unions a federal organizing and bargaining framework in the many states that currently deny public employees collective bargaining, plus binding impasse resolution and dues deduction. Union membership and revenue would likely grow in those states.

Governments would lose unilateral control over pay, hours, and working conditions for their workforces in states with weak labor laws, and would face federal enforcement and lawsuits. Taxpayers in those states could bear higher public-service labor costs.
